claim: Sarcomas account for up to 20% of all paediatric malignancies.
source: Sarcomas although rare in adult patients account for up to 20% of all paediatric malignancies (Burningham et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burningham et al., 2012

claim: Sarcomas do not respond well to conventional therapeutic interventions.
source: These are often aggressive diseases which do not respond well to conventional therapeutic interventions (Anderson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2012

claim: Many fusion protein generating aberrations occur in a genomic background with few co-occurring genetic alterations.
source: Significantly, many fusion protein generating aberrations occur in a genomic background with few co-occurring genetic alterations (Gao et al., 2018; Brohl et al., 2014; Tirode et al., 2014; Crompton et al., 2014; Seki et al., 2015; Shern et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: Gene fusions are often the primary driver of disease development in sarcomas.
source: This has led to the prevailing notion that these gene fusions are often the primary driver of disease development.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of few co-occurring genetic alterations

claim: Synovial sarcoma accounts for ~10% of soft-tissue sarcomas.
source: Synovial sarcoma is a fusion gene driven malignancy, which accounts for ~10% of soft-tissue sarcomas.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge without specific citation in this sentence

claim: Synovial sarcoma is particularly common in children and young adults with a peak incidence between 20–30 years of age.
source: It occurs in patients of all ages, but is particularly common in children and young adults with a peak incidence between 20–30 years of age.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The hallmark genetic abnormality in synovial sarcoma is a recurrent t(X;18) chromosomal rearrangement.
source: The hallmark genetic abnormality in synovial sarcoma is a recurrent t(X;18) chromosomal rearrangement.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The t(X;18) chromosomal rearrangement fuses the SS18 gene on chromosome 18 to one of three related genes SSX1, SSX2 and SSX4 on the X chromosome.
source: This fuses the SS18 gene (also known as SYT) on chromosome 18 to one of three related genes SSX1, SSX2 and SSX4 on the X chromosome(Clark et al., 1994; de Leeuw et al., 1995; Skytting, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 1994; de Leeuw et al., 1995; Skytting, 1999

claim: Essentially 100% of synovial sarcoma tumours contain an SS18-SSX fusion.
source: As such, essentially 100% of synovial sarcoma tumours contain an SS18-SSX fusion.
evidence: Based on the fact that the fusion is pathognomonic and used for diagnosis

claim: The SS18-SSX rearrangement is often the only genetic abnormality in synovial sarcoma tumours.
source: The SS18-SSX rearrangement is often the only genetic abnormality in synovial sarcoma tumours (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Barretina et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Barretina et al., 2010

claim: The SS18-SSX rearrangement is the primary driver of synovial sarcoma disease.
source: The SS18-SSX rearrangement is often the only genetic abnormality in synovial sarcoma tumours (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Barretina et al., 2010); suggesting that it is the primary driver of disease.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that it is often the only genetic abnormality

claim: Conditional expression of SS18-SSX in muscle progenitor cells leads to development of a fully penetrant synovial sarcoma like disease in mice.
source: Indeed, conditional expression of SS18-SSX in muscle progenitor cells leads to development of a fully penetrant synovial sarcoma like disease in mice (Haldar et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haldar et al., 2007

claim: The SS18-SSX fusion protein is believed to function as an aberrant transcriptional regulator.
source: The SS18-SSX fusion protein is believed to function as an aberrant transcriptional regulator.
evidence: Stated as current understanding in the field

claim: The SS18 protein is a dedicated component of the chromatin remodelling BAF complex which functions primarily in transcriptional activation.
source: The SS18 protein is a dedicated component of the chromatin remodelling BAF (also known as SWI/SNF) complex which functions primarily in transcriptional activation (Middeljans et al., 2012; Kadoch and Crabtree, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Middeljans et al., 2012; Kadoch and Crabtree, 2013

claim: The SSX proteins are thought to function in gene silencing, potentially through interactions with the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC)1.
source: Whereas the SSX proteins are thought to function in gene silencing; potentially through interactions with the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC)1 (Lim et al., 1998; Soulez et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lim et al., 1998; Soulez et al., 1999

claim: SS18-SSX dominantly assembles into BAF complexes in synovial sarcoma cells, leading to eviction of the wildtype SS18 and SNF5 proteins from the complex.
source: SS18-SSX dominantly assembles into BAF complexes in synovial sarcoma cells, leading to eviction of the wildtype SS18 and SNF5 proteins from the complex.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The altered SS18-SSX containing BAF complex is redistributed on chromatin and drives an expression signature required to maintain the proliferative/undifferentiated state of synovial sarcoma cells.
source: This altered complex assembly is redistributed on chromatin and drives an expression signature required to maintain the proliferative/undifferentiated state of synovial sarcoma cells (McBride et al., 2018; Banito et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to McBride et al., 2018; Banito et al., 2018

claim: SS18-SSX chromatin binding is directed in part through interactions with the PRC1.1 complex, mediated by the SSX portion of the fusion.
source: SS18-SSX chromatin binding is directed in part through interactions with the PRC1.1 complex; mediated by the SSX portion of the fusion (Banito et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Banito et al., 2018

claim: The recruitment of SS18-SSX to chromatin via interactions with PRC1.1 is essential for the oncogenic function of the fusion.
source: The recruitment of SS18-SSX to chromatin via interactions with PRC1.1 is essential for the oncogenic function of the fusion.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Recruitment of BAF complex activity to SS18-SSX bound regions is essential for transcriptional activation of fusion target genes.
source: Recruitment of BAF complex activity to SS18-SSX bound regions is essential for transcriptional activation of fusion target genes (McBride et al., 2018; Banito et al., 2018; Kadoch et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to McBride et al., 2018; Banito et al., 2018; Kadoch et al., 2017

claim: Depletion of SS18-SSX protein levels leads to reduced BAF complex binding at target sites and repression of fusion target genes.
source: Depletion of SS18-SSX protein levels leads to reduced BAF complex binding at target sites and repression of fusion target genes.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Three independent sgRNAs targeting the bromodomain of BRD9 were depleted from synovial, but not Ewing sarcoma cell cultures.
source: These analyses demonstrated that three independent sgRNAs targeting the bromodomain of BRD9 were depleted from synovial, but not Ewing sarcoma cell cultures (Figure 1B–C, and Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C and source data

claim: Of the 52 bromodomains contained within 38 proteins targeted in the library, only the BRD9 bromodomain had all sgRNAs specifically depleted in synovial sarcoma cells.
source: Remarkably, of the 52 bromodomains contained within 38 proteins targeted in this library, only the BRD9 bromodomain had all sgRNAs specifically depleted in synovial sarcoma cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: BRD9 bromodomain targeting sgRNAs were only depleted in synovial sarcoma cells, not in Ewing or rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines.
source: These experiments demonstrated that BRD9 bromodomain targeting sgRNAs were only depleted in synovial sarcoma cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and source data 3

claim: The sgRNAs targeting BRD9 have comparable or higher genome editing efficiencies in Ewing and rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines, compared to synovial sarcoma cells.
source: Importantly, the sgRNAs used here have comparable or higher genome editing efficiencies in Ewing and rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines, compared to synovial sarcoma cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: BRD9 expression levels are consistent across all cell lines tested.
source: Moreover, BRD9 expression levels are consistent across all cell lines tested, indicating that differences in BRD9 levels do not reflect altered sensitivity to BRD9 targeting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: shRNA-based knockdown of BRD9 shows similar synovial sarcoma specific effects.
source: Using an independent shRNA-based approach we observed similar synovial sarcoma specific effects following knockdown of BRD9 protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-G

claim: Among almost 400 cancer cell lines assayed in Project DRIVE, synovial sarcoma cell lines are the most sensitive to BRD9 targeting.
source: Consistent with this, within the recently published Project DRIVE (McDonald et al., 2017) database we observe, that among the almost 400 cancer cell lines assayed, synovial sarcoma cell lines are the most sensitive to BRD9 targeting (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data from Project DRIVE database shown in Figure 1E

claim: Only wildtype full-length BRD9 can rescue the depletion of sgRNAs targeting the bromodomain.
source: This demonstrated that only wildtype full-length BRD9 can rescue the depletion of sgRNAs targeting the bromodomain (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and related figures

claim: BRD9 and the BRD9 bromodomain are selective functional dependencies in synovial sarcoma.
source: This indicates that BRD9, and the BRD9 bromodomain, are selective functional dependencies in synovial sarcoma; highlighting a novel therapeutic target in this disease.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments and specificity data

claim: BRD9 has previously been shown to be a component of the BAF complex in several normal tissues.
source: BRD9 has previously been shown to be a component of the BAF complex in several normal tissues (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kadoch et al., 2013

claim: Biochemical studies in HEK293T cells have indicated that BRD9 can associate with SS18-SSX containing complexes.
source: Moreover, biochemical studies in HEK293T cells have indicated that BRD9 can also associate with SS18-SSX containing complexes in this setting (Middeljans et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Middeljans et al., 2012

claim: BRD9 associates with exogenously expressed SS18-SSX1/2 in HEK293T cells.
source: Consistent with previous results we found that BRD9 associates with exogenously expressed SS18-SSX1/2 in HEK293T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C,Figure 2-figure supplement-source data 1–3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: BRD9 co-purifies with endogenous SS18-SSX containing BAF complexes in synovial sarcoma cells.
source: Significantly, these experiments demonstrated that BRD9 co-purifies with endogenous SS18-SSX containing BAF complexes in synovial sarcoma cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and related figures

claim: SS18-SSX fusion proteins co-purify with BRD9 in reciprocal endogenous IP experiments.
source: Moreover, SS18-SSX fusion proteins co-purify with BRD9 in reciprocal endogenous IP experiments (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: BRD9 is a member of a novel subclass of BAF complex(es), termed GBAF (for GLTSCR1/1L-BAF).
source: A recent report indicates that BRD9 is a member of a novel subclass of BAF complex(es), termed GBAF (for GLTSCR1/1L-BAF) (Alpsoy and Dykhuizen, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alpsoy and Dykhuizen, 2018

claim: GBAF complexes lack SNF5 and an ARID component and contain BRD9, GLTSCR1 or GLTSCR1L as defining complex members.
source: These complexes lack SNF5 and an ARID component and contain BRD9, GLTSCR1 or GLTSCR1L as defining complex members.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge from the cited report

claim: Proteomic analysis of endogenous SS18-SSX containing complexes identified peptides mapping to GLTSCR1.
source: Our proteomic analysis of endogenous SS18-SSX containing complexes identified peptides mapping to GLTSCR1, lending support to the notion that the fusion incorporates into GBAF assemblies containing BRD9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: Core BAF complex members such as SMARCC1, SMARCC2 and SMARCA4 have relative abundances approximately equal to, or greater than, SS18-SSX.
source: This showed that core complex members such as SMARCC1, SMARCC2 and SMARCA4 have relative abundances approximately equal to, or greater than, SS18-SSX (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E using iBAQ algorithm

claim: The relative abundance of BRD9 (and GLTSCR1) is 10–20% that of SS18-SSX.
source: However, the relative abundance of BRD9 (and GLTSCR1) is 10–20% that of SS18-SSX; indicating that these components are sub-stoichiometric members of SS18-SSX containing complexes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from iBAQ analysis

claim: BRD9 and GLTSCR1 are sub-stoichiometric members of SS18-SSX containing complexes.
source: However, the relative abundance of BRD9 (and GLTSCR1) is 10–20% that of SS18-SSX; indicating that these components are sub-stoichiometric members of SS18-SSX containing complexes.
evidence: Inferred from the relative abundance measurements

claim: No robust dependencies were evident among the bromodomains of PBRM, SMARCA2 and SMARCA4 in the functional genomics screen.
source: However, no robust dependencies were evident among the bromodomains of these proteins which were targeted within our library (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: The minor subset of BRD9 containing complexes are particularly important and perhaps functionally specialised in synovial sarcoma cells.
source: Intriguingly, this suggests that the minor subset of BRD9 containing complexes are particularly important, and perhaps functionally specialised in synovial sarcoma cells.
evidence: Inferred from the specificity of BRD9 dependency despite its sub-stoichiometric presence

claim: High-density CRISPR mutagenesis identified an additional hotspot of sgRNA depletion within amino acids 311–345 of BRD9.
source: However, we identified an additional hotspot of sgRNA depletion within a previously uncharacterised central region of BRD9 (amino acids 311–345).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from high-density CRISPR mutagenesis

claim: A Δ311–345 BRD9 cDNA was incapable of rescuing the depletion of sgRNAs targeting the 311-345 region.
source: We confirmed the importance of this region with functional rescue experiments showing that a Δ311–345 BRD9 cDNA was incapable of rescuing the depletion of sgRNAs targeting this region (Figure 2G and Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: The BRD9 bromodomain is dispensable for BAF complex interaction.
source: Strikingly, co-IP experiments found that while the BRD9 bromodomain is dispensable for BAF complex interaction, this novel functional region is essential for association with the complex (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: The amino acids 311-345 region of BRD9 is essential for association with the BAF complex.
source: Strikingly, co-IP experiments found that while the BRD9 bromodomain is dispensable for BAF complex interaction, this novel functional region is essential for association with the complex (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: Association of BRD9 with the BAF complex is functionally essential in synovial sarcoma cells.
source: These results identify a novel BAF complex interaction domain within BRD9 and demonstrate that association of BRD9 with the BAF complex is functionally essential in synovial sarcoma cells.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing the 311-345 region is essential

claim: BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 bind broadly throughout the genome.
source: ChIP-seq analyses demonstrated that BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 bind broadly throughout the genome (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A

claim: ~35% of BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 binding sites occur at gene promoters and the remaining ~65% at distal inter- and intragenic regions.
source: with ~35% of binding sites occurring at gene promoters and the remaining ~65% at distal inter- and intragenic regions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B

claim: BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 co-localize extensively on the synovial sarcoma genome.
source: Comparing the binding profiles of BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 demonstrated that these proteins co-localize extensively on the synovial sarcoma genome.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis

claim: A clear majority of all identified BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 binding sites overlap.
source: Indeed, a clear majority of all identified BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 binding sites overlap (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C

claim: There is a tight correlation in BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 occupancy genome-wide.
source: and there is a tight correlation in BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 occupancy genome-wide (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 bind virtually all active gene promoters and enhancer elements.
source: Additional ChIP-seq analyses of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) and the histone modification H3K27Ac further demonstrates that BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 bind virtually all active gene promoters and enhancer elements (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: There is significant overlap between previous SS18-SSX1 ChIP studies and the epitope tag knock-in mediated SS18-SSX1 and BRD9 ChIP-seq experiments.
source: Importantly, we found a significant overlap between these previous SS18-SSX1 ChIP studies and our own epitope tag knock-in mediated SS18-SSX1 and BRD9 ChIP-seq experiments (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Synovial sarcoma cells were more sensitive to BRD9 bromodomain inhibition compared to other pediatric sarcomas.
source: Consistent with our genetic data, synovial sarcoma cells were more sensitive to BRD9 bromodomain inhibition compared to other pediatric sarcomas (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by dose response experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The effects of BRD9 bromodomain inhibition were modest with growth IC50 values in the μM range.
source: However, these effects were modest with growth IC50 values in the μM range.
evidence: Supported by dose response experimental data

claim: The chromatin occupancy of BRD9 is reduced in BI7273 treated cells but some BRD9 remains associated with chromatin.
source: Interestingly, spike-in normalized BRD9 ChIP-seq (ChIP-Rx) performed in BI7273 treated cells demonstrated that while the chromatin occupancy of BRD9 is reduced in inhibitor treated cells some BRD9 remains associated with chromatin (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Rx experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: BRD9 does not rely exclusively on bromodomain function to associate with chromatin.
source: This indicates that BRD9 does not rely exclusively on bromodomain function to associate with chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BRD9 remains on chromatin after bromodomain inhibition

claim: Mutational inactivation of the BRD9 bromodomain leads to an incomplete loss of BRD9 binding across the genome.
source: Consistent with this, mutational inactivation of the BRD9 bromodomain also leads to an incomplete loss of BRD9 binding across the genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: The ability of BRD9 to incorporate into the BAF complex is required for chromatin association.
source: Significantly, the ability of BRD9 to incorporate into the BAF complex is required for chromatin association, since deleting the BAF complex interaction domain (aa311-345) leads to a similar reduction in chromatin binding as bromodomain deletion (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: BRD9, as part of the BAF complex, can access chromatin in a bromodomain independent manner.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that BRD9, as part of the BAF complex, can access chromatin in a bromodomain independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BAF complex interaction is required for chromatin binding

claim: Bromodomain inhibition is unlikely to completely ablate the functional contributions of BRD9.
source: Highlighting that bromodomain inhibition, while at least partially effective at blocking synovial sarcoma cell growth/survival, is unlikely to completely ablate the functional contributions of BRD9.
evidence: Inferred from the incomplete loss of BRD9 chromatin binding with bromodomain inhibition

claim: dBRD9-A is a highly specific binder of the BRD9 bromodomain.
source: Importantly, dBRD9-A is a highly specific binder of the BRD9 bromodomain (Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by Bromoscan data shown in Figure 4E

claim: dBRD9-A elicits near complete BRD9 degradation at low nanomolar concentrations.
source: and elicits near complete BRD9 degradation at low nanomolar concentrations (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The degradation effects of dBRD9-A are dependent on the E3 ubiquitin ligase component CRBN.
source: These degradation effects are dependent on the E3 ubiquitin ligase component CRBN, as well as BRD9 bromodomain engagement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: The degradation effects of dBRD9-A are dependent on BRD9 bromodomain engagement.
source: These degradation effects are dependent on the E3 ubiquitin ligase component CRBN, as well as BRD9 bromodomain engagement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: Essentially no BRD9 remains bound on chromatin following 24 hr of dBRD9-A treatment.
source: Indeed, essentially no BRD9 remains bound on chromatin following 24 hr of dBRD9-A treatment (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Rx data shown in Figure 4H

claim: BRD9 degradation leads to a greater therapeutic response than bromodomain inhibition.
source: Significantly, BRD9 degradation leads to a greater therapeutic response than bromodomain inhibition (Figure 4I)
evidence: Supported by dose response data shown in Figure 4I

claim: Other pediatric sarcoma subtypes are unaffected by BRD9 degradation.
source: Moreover, consistent with our genetic data other pediatric sarcoma subtypes are unaffected by BRD9 degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F

claim: The observed increase in therapeutic response in dBRD9-A treated cells is not due to destabilisation of the SS18-SSX fusion itself.
source: Interestingly, the observed increase in therapeutic response in dBRD9-A treated cells is not due to destabilisation of the SS18-SSX fusion itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G

claim: The GBAF members (GLTSCR1/L), in addition to BRD9, are lost from fusion protein containing complexes following BRD9 degradation.
source: However, quantitative interactions proteomics of SS18-SSX containing complexes in dBRD9-A treated cells demonstrate that the GBAF members (GLTSCR1/L), in addition to BRD9, are lost from fusion protein containing complexes following BRD9 degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H

claim: BRD9 is essential for the proper assembly of GBAF complexes.
source: This suggests that BRD9 is essential for the proper assembly of GBAF complexes; and that BRD9 degradation specifically disrupts this subclass of SS18-SSX containing complexes.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of GLTSCR1/L from complexes following BRD9 degradation

claim: BRD9 degradation specifically disrupts the GBAF subclass of SS18-SSX containing complexes.
source: This suggests that BRD9 is essential for the proper assembly of GBAF complexes; and that BRD9 degradation specifically disrupts this subclass of SS18-SSX containing complexes.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of GLTSCR1/L from complexes following BRD9 degradation

claim: Targeting BRD9 function with chemical degraders is a more efficacious therapeutic approach in synovial sarcoma than bromodomain inhibitors.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that targeting BRD9 function with chemical degraders, rather than bromodomain inhibitors, is a more efficacious therapeutic approach in synovial sarcoma.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of degrader and inhibitor effects

claim: Synovial sarcoma cells treated with dBRD9-A undergo a progressive cell cycle arrest.
source: Synovial sarcoma cells treated with dBRD9-A undergo a progressive cell cycle arrest (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5A

claim: dBRD9-A treatment is associated with an increase in Annexin–V positivity.
source: which is further associated with an increase in Annexin–V positivity (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis analysis data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Swapping the BRD9 bromodomain for the closely related BRD7 bromodomain renders BRD9 and synovial sarcoma cells insensitive to dBRD9-A treatment.
source: Consistent with the on-target activity of dBRD9-A, swapping the BRD9 bromodomain for the closely related BRD7 bromodomain (63%, sequence identity) renders BRD9 and synovial sarcoma cells insensitive to dBRD9-A treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: Treatment of mice with dBRD9-A over 24 days inhibited tumour progression in a synovial sarcoma xenograft model.
source: Using an in vivo synovial sarcoma xenograft model, we found that treatment of mice with dBRD9-A over 24 days inhibited tumour progression (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 5C

claim: In vivo pharmacodynamic activity of dBRD9-A was confirmed by immunoblotting BRD9 in tumour tissue derived from vehicle and dBRD9-A treated mice.
source: We confirmed in vivo pharmacodynamic activity of dBRD9-A in this system by immunoblotting BRD9 in tumour tissue derived from vehicle and dBRD9-A treated mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Mice treated with dBRD9-A did not suffer any overt side effects associated with treatment, retaining a normal body weight and blood counts.
source: Mice treated with dBRD9-A did not suffer any overt side effects associated with treatment, retaining a normal body weight and blood counts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D and and Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source datas 2–3).
evidence: Supported by body weight and blood count data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D

claim: Degradation of BRD9 primarily leads to down regulated gene expression.
source: Strikingly, degradation of BRD9 primarily leads to down regulated gene expression (Figure 5E and Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Several genes associated with SEs in HSSYII cells including TWIST1 and TLE1 are known to play key functional roles in synovial sarcoma.
source: Consistent with this, several genes associated with SEs in HSSYII cells including TWIST1 (38) and TLE1 (22) are known to play key functional roles in synovial sarcoma (Figure 5F).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Expression of many SE-associated genes has previously been linked to primary synovial sarcoma tumour phenotypes, defining both clinical and biological characteristics.
source: Moreover, expression of many of these genes has previously been linked to primary synovial sarcoma tumour phenotypes, defining both clinical and biological characteristics (McBride et al., 2018; Banito et al., 2018; Francis et al., 2007; Sarver et al., 2015; Terry et al., 2007; Takahashi et al., 2014; Baird et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: SEs have higher BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 occupancy levels compared to typical enhancers.
source: SEs have higher BRD9 and SS18-SSX1 occupancy levels compared to typical enhancers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: BRD9 degradation leads to a preferential downregulation of SE associated gene expression.
source: and BRD9 degradation leads to a preferential downregulation of SE associated gene expression (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G

claim: SE-associated genes depend on SS18-SSX1 to maintain their expression.
source: Significantly, these genes depend on SS18-SSX1 to maintain their expression, since shRNA mediated knockdown of SS18-SSX1 leads to a collapse of SE associated gene expression (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data after SS18-SSX1 knockdown shown in Figure 5H

claim: dBRD9-A treatment and consequential downregulation of transcription is associated with reductions in SS18-SSX1 binding at SEs.
source: dBRD9-A treatment and consequential downregulation of transcription is further associated with reductions in SS18-SSX1 binding at SEs (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F

claim: BRD9 is required to maintain the SE associated oncogenic transcriptional program driven by SS18-SSX.
source: However, these data demonstrate that BRD9 is required to maintain the SE associated oncogenic transcriptional program driven by SS18-SSX and the phenotypic impact of BRD9 degradation underlines the functional importance of this gene cohort.
evidence: Inferred from the preferential downregulation of SE genes and their dependence on SS18-SSX

claim: Targeting BRD9 using the degrader compound directly perturbs underlying oncogenic mechanisms in synovial sarcoma.
source: Most importantly, these data show that targeting BRD9 using our novel degrader compound directly perturbs underlying oncogenic mechanisms in this disease.
evidence: Inferred from the effects on SE-associated gene expression and tumor progression

claim: BRD9 supports oncogenic mechanisms underlying the SS18-SSX fusion in synovial sarcoma.
source: We demonstrate that BRD9 supports oncogenic mechanisms underlying the SS18-SSX fusion in synovial sarcoma and highlight targeted degradation of BRD9 as a potential therapeutic opportunity in this disease.
evidence: Inferred from all the experimental data showing BRD9's role in maintaining oncogenic gene expression

claim: Targeted degradation of BRD9 is a potential therapeutic opportunity in synovial sarcoma.
source: We demonstrate that BRD9 supports oncogenic mechanisms underlying the SS18-SSX fusion in synovial sarcoma and highlight targeted degradation of BRD9 as a potential therapeutic opportunity in this disease.
evidence: Inferred from the therapeutic effects observed with dBRD9-A

claim: BRD9 may promote and/or stabilize binding of SS18-SSX containing complexes at acetylated chromatin regions.
source: BRD9 may promote and/or stabilize binding of SS18-SSX containing complexes at acetylated chromatin regions; since loss of BRD9 can lead to reduced fusion protein occupancy at some super enhancers.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed reduction in SS18-SSX binding after BRD9 degradation
